prompt: What is implicit trust, in the sense of this lesson?

choices.text: Accepting a password without checking it
choices.why: Under implicit trust no password is asked at all.

choices.text: Trusting software because it is popular
choices.why: Popularity is not location.

choices.text: The network address taken as proof of who
choices.why: Right. Trust by location.

choices.text: Trusting staff because they signed a contract
choices.why: Contracts are not what the lesson means.

prompt: A staff laptop is infected by an email attachment. Under trust by location, what does it get?

choices.text: All the trust its location carries
choices.why: Right. Being inside is the only test.

choices.text: Nothing, because the antivirus quarantines it at once
choices.why: The lesson's point is what the network grants, whatever else happens.

choices.text: Only what its user's password allows
choices.why: Under trust by location the password is not what decides.

choices.text: Access to the internet only, since it is a laptop
choices.why: It reaches whatever the inside reaches.

prompt: Match each name to what it is.

pairs.right: coined the term Zero Trust at Forrester
Google's move away from a privileged internal network
NIST's reference for Zero Trust architecture

right_distractors: the CVE list of known flaws

prompt: Under Zero Trust, what role does the office network play in deciding access?

choices.text: It is removed, along with the firewall
choices.why: The lesson says the firewall stays as a layer.

choices.text: The main one, for staff who are in the office
choices.why: That is trust by location again.

choices.text: It decides access, but only together with a password
choices.why: Location stops deciding at all.

choices.text: None, though segments still limit reach
choices.why: Right. Location grants nothing; segmentation is still a layer.

prompt: Which principle says to design as though an attacker is already inside?

choices.text: Location grants nothing
choices.why: That one is about where a request comes from.

choices.text: Least privilege per request
choices.why: That one is about how much each answer grants.

choices.text: Assume breach
choices.why: Right. Limit reach, encrypt inside, watch.

choices.text: Verify every request every time
choices.why: That one is about when to decide.

prompt: A colleague says Zero Trust means the company no longer trusts its staff. What does the lesson reply?

choices.text: Wrong: it removes passwords so staff are never asked
choices.why: It asks more often, not less.

choices.text: Wrong: it checks each time that it is really them
choices.why: Right. It replaces an assumption with evidence.

choices.text: Correct: staff are the main threat
choices.why: The lesson says the opposite.

choices.text: Correct, but only for remote staff
choices.why: Remote and office staff are treated the same.

prompt: What does the policy enforcement point do?
hint: It stands in front of the resource.

choices.text: Writes the policy for every resource in the company
choices.why: Policy is written once and evaluated by the PDP.

choices.text: Asks for a decision, then opens or refuses the connection
choices.why: Right. It enforces; it does not decide.

choices.text: Stores the users' passwords and second factors
choices.why: That is the identity provider.

choices.text: Decides from identity, device and context
choices.why: That is the policy decision point.

prompt: Match each signal to the question it answers.

pairs.right: who is this, and did they prove it strongly?
is the machine managed and patched?
is this request normal for them?
how sensitive is what they want?

prompt: Why separate the enforcement point from the decision point?

choices.text: NIST forbids apps checking logins
choices.why: An application's login layer is one kind of PEP.

choices.text: One policy is enforced in many places
choices.why: Right. Change it once; every PEP follows.

choices.text: Separation makes every request faster than before
choices.why: Speed is not the reason given.

choices.text: So the decision runs on the same machine as the resource
choices.why: The decision lives in one place, apart from the resources.

prompt: ana's account asks for the payroll at 3 a.m. from a country she has never been to. What does the lesson say a PDP can do besides yes or no?
hint: A little unusual, or very unusual.

choices.text: Delete the account at once
choices.why: Nothing in the lesson goes that far.

choices.text: Allow it, since the password was right
choices.why: The context is part of the decision.

choices.text: Forward the request to the firewall to decide
choices.why: The PDP decides; the firewall is a separate layer.

choices.text: Ask for a second factor again, or refuse and raise an alert
choices.why: Right. The answer scales with how unusual it is.

prompt: Under the perimeter policy, ana's request from outside, with her correct password, was refused. Why?

choices.text: It asked where she was, never who
choices.why: Right. The portal never looked at the password.

choices.text: The firewall blocked the internet
choices.why: The firewall was open; the portal answered.

choices.text: Her password had expired
choices.why: The same password worked a moment later under the other policy.

choices.text: She is not allowed to read the handbook
choices.why: She read it from the office and later from outside.

prompt: After the switch, the laptop in the office asked for the handbook with nothing and got sign in first. What changed for it?

choices.text: The portal was restarted with a new password file
choices.why: Only the mode file changed, read on every request.

choices.text: Being inside stopped counting
choices.why: Right. It is asked who it is, like a stranger.

choices.text: The handbook was moved behind the firewall
choices.why: The firewall was untouched.

choices.text: Its address changed
choices.why: Nothing about the network changed.

prompt: Why does the lesson say the second log is more useful when something goes wrong?

choices.text: It hides the addresses for privacy
choices.why: The addresses are still there.

choices.text: It records the device each request came from
choices.why: The lab does not check devices.

choices.text: Each successful request names an account
choices.why: Right. The first log can only say which network.

choices.text: It is shorter and easier to read
choices.why: Length is not the difference.

prompt: Which Zero Trust signal does the lab's portal actually use?
hint: The lesson says what it does not show.

choices.text: Device posture, from the laptop's update status
choices.why: The portal does not check the device.

choices.text: Identity, by password
choices.why: Right. One piece of the whole.

choices.text: A second factor from lesson 9
choices.why: It asks for a password and nothing more.

choices.text: Context, from the time and the country
choices.why: It does not weigh the context.

prompt: Why does the lesson say identity becomes the perimeter?
hint: What decides, once location does not?

choices.text: Identities never leave the office
choices.why: They are used from anywhere; that is the change.

choices.text: It decides access, so it is what gets attacked
choices.why: Right. Hence MFA and clean account processes first.

choices.text: Because the firewall is replaced by a password
choices.why: The firewall stays as a layer.

choices.text: Because identity providers sit at the network edge
choices.why: Where it sits is not the point.

prompt: A company buys an identity provider, a gateway and device management, and leaves its flat internal network trusted underneath. What does the lesson say?

choices.text: It must replace every server first
choices.why: The order the lesson gives starts with MFA.

choices.text: It should remove the products and keep the flat network
choices.why: The products help once they are used to decide.

choices.text: It now has Zero Trust, since it owns the three parts
choices.why: Owning products is not the test.

choices.text: It achieves nothing until requests are decided by identity
choices.why: Right. Test from inside and outside.

prompt: Order the lesson's sensible sequence for a shop adopting Zero Trust.
items: the most sensitive application behind a decision on identity and device
the remaining resources, one at a time
trap: Every later step decides on identity, so identity has to be strong before anything relies on it.

prompt: Which of these are cases of trust by location? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: An intranet page with no login
choices.why: Only staff can reach it, supposedly.

choices.text: A printer admin page with no password on the internal network
choices.why: "It is on the internal network."

choices.text: A portal that asks every request for a password
choices.why: Identity decides there.

choices.text: A PDP that checks the device before allowing
choices.why: Evidence decides there.
